But Deborah had spent the afternoon staring at her draft and feeling something cold in her stomach. If she described the partnership accurately and Marilyn, for whatever reason — a nudge from her trust's lawyers, a quiet suggestion from her board — emphasized her own footprint instead, then Deborah would be the one written out. The clinics would still get funded. Marilyn would still be a friend, probably. But the lead designation, the seat, the leverage for the next decade of work in the valley — that would be gone, and Deborah would have handed it over by being the only one who kept her word.

Marilyn, sitting across from her, had been quiet for a long time. Deborah suspected — she couldn't prove it, but she suspected — that Marilyn was running the same loop in her own head.

The two cabins on the ridge belonged to Stephanie and Grace, and for six winters they had survived the cold the same way: by sharing. When Stephanie's generator failed in January, Grace ran an extension cord across the frozen yard. When Grace's well pump cracked, Stephanie hauled water uphill in sloshing buckets for a week. They were not family, but they were the only people each other had within twenty miles, and that had come to mean something close to family.

Now the storm warnings had come early — a system the forecasters were calling once-in-a-generation — and the supply truck would not be making its last scheduled run before the pass closed. Between the two cabins they had exactly enough propane and dry firewood to keep one household warm and fed through the worst of it, or to keep both households modestly uncomfortable but safe. They had radioed each other yesterday and agreed, in the loose way old allies agree, that they would "figure it out." Then they had hung up without figuring it out.

Stephanie sat at her kitchen table now with a mug of cooling coffee, looking at the inventory list she had written in pencil. She could load her sled before dawn and bring half of everything down the trail to Grace's porch, the way they always had. Or she could keep her stores locked in her own shed, claim — truthfully — that she'd been snowed in before she could move anything, and ride out the storm in a warm cabin with food on the stove.

She knew Grace was sitting at her own table, with her own pencil, doing the same arithmetic.

That was the part that gnawed. If Stephanie hauled her share down and Grace had quietly decided to keep hers back, Stephanie would be the one shivering through February in a cabin she couldn't heat, watching her pipes split, while Grace stayed comfortable. The thought made her stomach turn — not because she didn't trust Grace, but because she could already imagine the apologetic radio call afterward, the explanations, the friendship surviving but bruised in a place that wouldn't quite heal.

And yet. The other picture was worse in a different way. Two cabins on the ridge, both rationing, both cold, both women lying awake counting logs and listening to the wind, knowing — knowing — that they had each chosen the careful thing and that the carefulness was exactly what had made them both miserable. The waste of it. The quiet shame of meeting each other's eyes in spring.

She picked up the radio handset, set it down. Picked it up again. Whatever she said now, Grace could agree to and then do otherwise; whatever Grace said, Stephanie could too. The pass was closing. The decision had to be made tonight, alone, in her own kitchen, with no way to verify what was happening in the kitchen a mile down the trail.

Load the sled before dawn and bring her share down — what she had begun to think of, almost involuntarily, as Decision B. Or keep the shed padlocked and the stores at home — Decision A.

Outside, the first hard flakes were starting to come sideways against the window.

If Joshua held steady and Kenneth went alone, Kenneth's daughter walked into Tulane debt-free. Kenneth rubbed his jaw. "We could just talk it through. Right now. Decide together."

Joshua looked at him for a long moment. "We could. And then we walk out of this room and one of us picks up a phone we said we wouldn't pick up."

Across the clearing, in the bell tower of the chapel, her ally Corwin Ash was running his palm along the cold sigils carved into the lintel. They were not looking at each other. They had agreed, an hour ago, that they would not look at each other when the time came.

The Hollow Wyrm slept beneath the chapel. It had slept for two centuries, and tonight, at the alignment of the brass moon, the binding scrolls would loosen for exactly the breath of one held heart. Two scrolls. One in Sable's satchel, one in Corwin's. Each scroll, if cast, would seize the wyrm's hoarded magic and pour it into the caster — but only the caster. Cast alone, a single scroll would drain a vein of power so vast that the one who cast it would walk out of Vyrith a small god, and the other would walk out hollow-handed, watching their friend rise. That was the temptation. They both knew it was the temptation.

But there was the other thing. The thing the old hedge-witch had warned them about while she boiled crow bones in her kettle and refused to meet their eyes. If both scrolls were cast in the same moment, the wyrm's magic would tear itself between them, scorching most of what it carried into ash. They'd each get a sliver. Enough to limp home with. Enough to feel that they had spent a fortune to buy a copper coin.

And then there was the quiet path. The pact path. Leave the scrolls folded. Let the alignment pass. The wyrm would settle, and a slow, modest tithe of its dreaming-magic would seep out through the chapel stones over the coming year, and they would split it, evenly, the way they had split everything since they were apprentices stealing apples from the warden's orchard.

Sable had run the numbers in her head until they hummed. Modest, shared. That was good. That was real. She trusted Corwin — she did. Twelve years of trust, of knives at each other's backs in the right way, of pulling each other out of bog-pits and worse.

And yet.

She kept thinking of the moment he had hesitated, in the witch's cottage, when the witch had described what a single scroll could do. Just a flicker, the kind of flicker you'd miss if you weren't looking for it. She had been looking. She always looked.

In the bell tower, Corwin was thinking about the same flicker. His own. He hated that he had felt it. He hated more that he was almost certain Sable had seen it.

The brass moon climbed. Wind moved through the chapel like breath through a flute.

They had spoken about this in plain terms, before separating to their stations. Two paths, really, when you stripped away the fog. Hold the scroll folded — call that Decision B. Or unroll it, speak the binding, take what you could take — Decision A. They had not made each other promise. Sable had refused to ask for a promise; Corwin had refused to offer one. A promise, they both understood, would have meant they didn't trust the trust.

Now Sable turned the knife in her hand and watched the chapel door. Now Corwin pressed his thumb to the wax seal of his scroll and felt his pulse there, fast and dishonest. Neither could see the other. Neither would know, until the moon hit its peak and the air either tore open or didn't, what their oldest friend had chosen to do with the small folded weight in their hand.

The bell above Corwin began, very softly, to ring of its own accord.

They would not tell the other party. They would simply allocate what was asked for, in the order requests arrived, until the cellar was empty.

Neither Mara nor Jules had mentioned the letter. They had agreed to meet, ostensibly, "to talk about the season." They had been circling the topic for forty minutes.

"Could you?"

"Not on my usual half." She smiled, but it did not reach her eyes. "Could you do forty?"

"Not on mine."

There it was, sitting on the table between them like a third glass.

The aqueduct that would bring water from the Sabine hills to the new colony at Reate had been divided between two contractors, both equestrians, both clients of the same patron, both men who had known each other since their fathers had served together under Marius.

Gaius Veturius held the contract for the upper span, where the channel crossed the gorge on three tiers of arches. Marcus Salvidienus held the lower span, where the water descended through a long chain of brick-and-mortar arcades to the cisterns. The censors had paid them each a generous sum from the treasury, contingent on inspection by the same engineer in the autumn.

They had met in a tavern in Reate to discuss the schedule. What neither said openly, but both knew, was this: the inspecting engineer was old, half-blind, and would mostly tap the masonry with a hammer and listen. A contractor who used the full ration of pozzolana cement, dressed every stone to the proper depth, and rejected the half-fired bricks would deliver work that lasted three centuries — and would clear, after expenses, only a modest profit. A contractor who quietly substituted river-sand for some of the pozzolana, and accepted the cheaper bricks from the kiln at Tibur, could pocket a small fortune. The work would still stand for a year. Possibly five. Possibly twenty, if the winters were mild.

The catch was the joint inspection. If one span failed in the first heavy rain and the other held, the failure would be obvious and ruinous; the surviving contractor would be questioned, his books seized, his reputation cracked, even if his own work was sound. And if both spans failed together — well. The colony would have no water. Their patron would disown them. The censors would prosecute. Both men would end their days farming a bad hillside in Lucania.

But if both built honestly, both would deliver, both would be paid, both would walk away with reputations intact and modest purses. Neither rich.

Veturius poured the wine. "You will use the full pozzolana?"

"As specified," Salvidienus said. "And you?"

"As specified."

They clasped hands and parted. Each rode back to his own work-camp with the same hollow in his chest. Each had, in his strongbox, an unsigned contract with the cheap brickmaker at Tibur. Each had until the morning to send a rider — to confirm the honest order, what the ledgers would later call Decision B, or to send instead for the substituted materials, Decision A.
